chapters.title: A Spark in the Mountains
beats: In northern Yemen, decades of political and sectarian friction set the state against armed religious revivalists after the 1962 revolution dismantled the old Zaidi Imamate.

A local dispute escalated into full-scale combat when state security forces launched an offensive against mountain strongholds, drawing neighbouring powers and international shipping lanes into an expanding theatre of war.
What began as a security crackdown to capture a single dissident cleric steadily broadened into widespread warfare that shook the Arabian Peninsula.
How did an arrest operation in northern Yemen trigger a wider regional conflict?

chapters.title: Old Grievances, New Rifts
beats: The rugged mountains of Saada Governorate hold deep symbolic weight for Yemen's Zaidi community, which had governed the northern highlands for over a millennium before losing power in the 1962 revolution.
President Ali Abdullah Saleh sought to consolidate national control over the divided country, relying on Wahhabi allies to defeat southern secessionists during the 1994 civil war.
Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi, a former parliamentarian and charismatic religious figure, rallied northern Zaidis against government policies, adopting an official anti-American slogan in 2003.
When Hussein's followers staged mass protests in the capital, Sanaa, Saleh saw the growing movement as an intolerable challenge to his centralized authority.

Meanwhile, young commander Abdul-Malik al-Houthi stood ready within the movement's ranks, while Yemeni Foreign Minister Abu Bakr al-Qirbi managed the regime's fragile diplomatic ties across the Middle East.

chapters.title: 18 June 2004
beats: On 18 June 2004, Yemeni police arrested 640 followers of Hussein al-Houthi demonstrating outside the Great Mosque of Sanaa, prompting President Ali Abdullah Saleh to dispatch government forces to capture the cleric.
Two days later, on 20 June 2004, the Yemeni government placed a $55,000 bounty on Hussein al-Houthi's head and ordered a comprehensive military operation to crush his alleged rebellion.
Heavy fighting erupted across the northern rugged terrain from June to August 2004, leaving between 500 and 1,000 people dead as government troops closed in on the mountain caves.
The opening campaign reached its climax on 10 September 2004, when Yemeni security forces tracked down and killed Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi in Saada Governorate.
chapters.hook: The government believed the rebellion had died with its founder, but leadership in the northern mountains had already changed hands.

chapters.title: The Resurgence
beats: Hussein's younger brother, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, assumed command of the insurgent ranks as fresh clashes between March and April 2005 left around 1,500 people dead across northern Yemen.
President Ali Abdullah Saleh offered a presidential pardon in May 2005, but rebel leaders rejected the offer when the government refused their counter-conditions for surrender.
By 21 May 2005, official estimates tabulated 552 fatalities, 2,708 wounded, and over US$ 270 million in infrastructure and economic damages caused by the widening conflict.

Seeking political advantage, Saleh announced in July 2005 he would not contest the 2006 presidential elections, claiming political parties should find young leaders to compete in elections to establish ground for a peaceful transfer of power.

Saleh pardoned jailed insurgents and freed over 600 captured Shi'a fighters in March 2006, but subsequently reversed his retirement decision, citing popular pressure, and won the September 2006 election with 77.2% of the vote.
The brief political pause collapsed on 28 January 2007 when militants struck military installations in Saada Governorate, leaving six government soldiers dead and twenty wounded.

chapters.title: Operation Scorched Earth
beats: By April 2008, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees reported that fighting in Sa'dah Governorate had displaced an estimated 77,000 residents.
Violence struck religious sites on 2 May 2008 when a bombing at the Bin Salman Mosque in Saada killed 15 worshippers and wounded 55 as civilians exited Friday prayers.
On 11 August 2009, Saleh unleashed Operation Scorched Earth, sending government tanks and fighter jets into Sa'ada province to root out Abdul-Malik al-Houthi's mountain networks.
The regional dimension exploded on 4 November 2009 when Houthi fighters crossed the northern border into Saudi Arabia, killing a border guard and seizing Al Khubah Village.

Saudi forces retaliated with artillery barrages and a naval blockade, while Iranian naval vessels arrived in the Gulf of Aden and Yemeni naval patrols intercepted an arms-laden Iranian vessel along the Red Sea coast.

Yemeni Foreign Minister Abu Bakr al-Qirbi publicly confronted Tehran on 13 December 2009, demanding that Iranian authorities stop religious groups from funneling financial and material aid to northern rebels.
chapters.hook: With foreign militaries engaged and regional waters patrolled by rival navies, the battle ground down to a standstill along the rugged border.

chapters.title: A Fragile Halt
beats: In early January 2010, the Houthis nominated Iraqi Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani as mediator, though the Yemeni military pressed ahead on 13 January with Operation Blow to the Head to capture Sa'adah city.

As Saudi military fatalities reached 133 dead by 22 January, rebel commander Abdul-Malik al-Houthi declared a unilateral truce on 25 January 2010, offering a full withdrawal from Saudi territory to protect civilian life.

Despite sporadic skirmishes through the summer of 2010 that killed dozens of tribal fighters in Souffian, a formal ceasefire agreement was concluded in 2010, bringing an intermittent halt to the fighting between the Houthis and the Yemeni government.

The conflict transformed the geopolitical landscape: Ali Abdullah Saleh had buried Hussein al-Houthi at Sana'a central prison in 2004 to prevent his grave becoming a shrine, while King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia ordered 10,000 homes built in Jizan in 2008 to shelter displaced border residents.
